group.title: Shopping
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To go to stores and buy things.
examples: We {shop} at the market on Saturday.
wrong: I shop at the store by selling my things.

words.meaning: To go to stores to buy things.
wrong: I go shopping when I want to stay at home.

words.meaning: Money used in the US and some other countries. It has 100 cents.
wrong: A dollar is a kind of fruit.

words.meaning: A very small coin. There are 100 in a dollar.
wrong: One cent is more money than ten dollars.

words.meaning: Words you use to ask the price of something.
wrong: How much is the color of your hair?

words.meaning: A list of things you need to buy.
examples: Milk and eggs are on my {shopping list}.
wrong: I wrote a song on my shopping list and sang it.

words.meaning: A bag you carry the things you buy in.
examples: Put the apples in the {shopping bag}.
wrong: I wear my shopping bag on my head as a hat.

words.meaning: A big metal basket on wheels that you push in a store.
examples: Push the {shopping cart} to the checkout.
wrong: I fly the shopping cart over the store.

words.meaning: Costing half of the normal money.
wrong: It is half price, so it costs two times more.

words.meaning: A thin bag you get in a store to carry what you buy.
wrong: I put my soup in a plastic bag and drink it with a straw.

words.meaning: Two things of the same kind that you use together.
examples: I bought a new {pair} of socks.
wrong: A pair of shoes is just one shoe.

words.meaning: A weight of one thousand grams.
wrong: A kilo is how long a road is.

words.meaning: A glass pot with a lid for food.
wrong: A jar is a soft hat made of wool.

words.meaning: A small paper or plastic bag or box with food in it.
wrong: A packet is a large truck for moving houses.

words.meaning: The machine in a store that keeps the money when you pay.
examples: The woman put my money in the {cash register}.
wrong: I cook my eggs in the cash register.

words.meaning: Things you wear on your body, like shirts and pants.
wrong: I eat my clothes for breakfast.

words.meaning: A soft shirt with short arms and no buttons.
examples: He wears a white {T-shirt} in summer.
wrong: I wear my T-shirt on my feet.

words.meaning: Strong blue pants made of cotton.
examples: These {jeans} are too long for me.
wrong: I put my jeans on my head to keep my ears warm.

words.meaning: Polite words to ask someone for help or attention.
wrong: Excuse me, I shouted, and pushed the man out of the way.

words.meaning: Words you say when you give something to someone.
examples: {Here you are}, your change is two dollars.
wrong: Here you are, she said, and kept the money in her hand.

words.meaning: Words you say when you decide to buy something.
examples: This bag is nice. {I’ll take it}.
wrong: I’ll take it, he said, and walked out without buying it.

words.meaning: A small room in a store where you try on clothes.
examples: You can try the dress in the {changing room}.
wrong: We cook dinner in the changing room.

words.meaning: A long path between shelves in a store.
wrong: I swim in the aisle of the store.

words.meaning: A person who gives you things for money.
wrong: The seller only buys things and never gives anything away.

words.meaning: A person who pays money for something.
wrong: The buyer got the money and gave nothing back.

words.meaning: A small table or shop at a market.
examples: She sells flowers at a {stall} in the market.
wrong: The stall is a big building with twenty floors.

words.meaning: A lower price for a short time.
examples: Buy two, get one free. It’s a {special offer}!
wrong: The special offer makes everything cost more.

words.meaning: A small plastic card you use to pay with money from your bank.
examples: Can I pay with my {bank card}?
wrong: I open the door of my house with my bank card and a key.

words.meaning: A box made of thick paper for milk or eggs.
wrong: The carton is made of heavy stone.

words.meaning: Bread that is made in one big piece.
wrong: A loaf of bread is one small crumb.

words.meaning: Costing more money than you want to pay.
examples: I can’t buy it. It’s {too expensive}.
wrong: It costs one cent, so it is too expensive for me.

words.meaning: The times when a store is open.
examples: The {opening hours} are nine to five.
wrong: The opening hours are the times when the store is closed.

words.meaning: Ready to be bought.
wrong: The house is for sale, but nobody can buy it.

words.meaning: Buying things on the internet.
examples: I do my {online shopping} on my phone.
wrong: I do my online shopping at the market with no phone.

words.meaning: Words you say when you do not want anything more.
wrong: That’s all, he said, and asked for ten more things.

words.meaning: To use a plastic bank card, not cash, to buy something.
wrong: I pay by card with coins from my pocket.

words.meaning: The big glass at the front of a store where things are shown.
examples: I saw a nice dress in the {shop window}.
wrong: I hid the shop window under my bed.

words.meaning: Food and things for the home that you buy at a store.
examples: Can you help me carry the {groceries}?
wrong: I wear my groceries to the party.

words.meaning: A group of twelve.
wrong: A dozen eggs is three eggs.

words.meaning: One thing in a list or a group of things.
wrong: I bought ten items, so I have only one thing.
